• ••Introduction••
	• The author, Warren W. Wiersbe, thanks readers for their encouragement and feedback on the "Be" series.
	• He mentions that he has received letters from readers around the world, including pastors, missionaries, and Sunday school teachers.
• ••Acknowledgments••
	• Wiersbe thanks Dr. Donald Burdick, Dr. Lloyd Perry, and Dr. Charles W. Koller for teaching him how to study the Bible and preach effectively.
	• He also thanks the late Dr. D. B. Eastep, who pastored the Calvary Baptist Church in Covington, Kentucky, and shared his ministry with him.
• ••The "Be" Series••
	• The "Be" series is a result of Wiersbe's experience as a pastor at Calvary Baptist Church.
	• The series is a by-product of Dr. Eastep's kindness and the church's love and encouragement.
• ••Key Theme and Verses••
	• The key theme of the "Be" series is "The King and His kingdom".
	• The key verses are Matthew 2:2 and 4:17.
• ••Outline of the Book••
	• The book is divided into five sections: The Revelation of the King, The Rebellion Against the King, The Retirement of the King, The Rejection of the King, and The Resurrection of the King.
	• Each section is further divided into sub-sections.
• ••Section I: The Revelation of the King (1-10)••
	• This section introduces the person, principles, and power of the King.
	• It covers Matthew 1-10.
• ••Section II: The Rebellion Against the King (11-13)••
	• This section describes the rejection of the King's messenger, works, principles, and person.
	• It covers Matthew 11-13.
• ••Section III: The Retirement of the King (14-20)••
	• This section describes the King's withdrawal from the crowds and his focus on his disciples.
	• It covers Matthew 14-20.
• ••Section IV: The Rejection of the King (21-27)••
	• This section describes the King's public presentation as King, conflict with rulers, prophetic message, suffering, and death.
	• It covers Matthew 21-27.
• ••Section V: The Resurrection of the King (28)••
	• This section describes the King's resurrection and the good news it brings.
	• It covers Matthew 28.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Matthew's Gospel••
	• Written to instruct Roman readers
	• Presents Christ as the perfect "Son of Man"
	• Focuses on the kingdom of heaven

â€¢ ••Matthew's Organization••
	• Divided into 10 sections with alternating "doing" and "teaching"
	• Each teaching section ends with a transitional statement
	• Chapters can be divided into narrative, teaching, and transition

â€¢ ••Matthew's Content••
	• Records at least 20 specific miracles
	• Includes six major messages:
		- Sermon on the Mount (chaps. 5-7)
		- Charge to the apostles (chap. 10)
		- Parables of the kingdom (chap. 13)
		- Lesson on forgiveness (chap. 18)
		- Denunciation of the Pharisees (chap. 23)
		- Prophetic discourse on the Mount of Olives (chaps. 24-25)

â€¢ ••Matthew's Focus••
	• Emphasizes the kingdom of heaven
	• Presents Jesus as the Doer and the Teacher

â€¢ ••The Kingdom of Heaven••
	• Message first preached by John the Baptist (Matt. 3:1-2)
	• Jesus also preached the message from the beginning of His ministry (Matt. 4:23)
	• Requires a moral and spiritual response from the people

â€¢ ••Matthew's Pattern••
	• Arranged material in a topical order, rather than chronological
	• Grouped 10 miracles together in chapters 8-9
	• Omitted certain events

â€¢ ••Matthew's Significance••
	• Introduced a new book, the New Testament
	• Introduced a new King, Jesus Christ
	• Introduced a new people, the church

â€¢ ••The Church••
	• Matthew is the only gospel writer to use the word "church" (Matt. 16:18; 18:17)
	• Refers to a local assembly of believers
	• Composed of both Jews and Gentiles

â€¢ ••The New Testament Church••
	• Different from the Old Testament Israel
	• Composed of both Jews and Gentiles
	• No racial or ethnic distinctions

â€¢ ••Matthew's Task••
	• To introduce a new people, the church
	• To present Jesus as the King of the kingdom of heaven

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Matthew's Universal Message••
	• Matthew's Gospel includes a universal element that includes Gentiles
	• Examples: Gentile leaders worshiping Jesus (Matt. 2:1-12), Jesus performing miracles for Gentiles (Matt. 8:5-13, 15:21-28)

â€¢ ••Gentile Inclusion in the Church••
	• The early church initially consisted only of believing Jews and Jewish proselytes (Acts 2-7)
	• The gospel spread to Samaria (Acts 8), and Gentiles became fully accepted in the church (Acts 10)
	• The Conference at Jerusalem (Acts 15) settled the decision that Gentiles did not have to become Jews to become Christians

â€¢ ••Matthew's Anticipation of Gentile Inclusion••
	• Matthew's Gospel anticipated the inclusion of Gentiles in the church
	• His book helped settle differences and create unity between Jews and Gentiles in the early church

â€¢ ••Matthew's Conversion and Call••
	• Matthew's old name was Levi, the son of Alphaeus (Mark 2:14)
	• He was a tax collector, a hated profession in Jewish society
	• His name "Matthew" means "the gift of God," commemorating his conversion and call to be a disciple

â€¢ ••Tax Collectors in Jewish Society••
	• Tax collectors were considered traitors and thieves
	• They were religiously suspect and unclean due to their constant contacts with Gentiles

â€¢ ••Jesus' View of Tax Collectors••
	• Jesus classified tax collectors with harlots and other sinners (Matt. 5:46-47, 18:17)
	• However, He was also the "friend of publicans and sinners" (Matt. 11:19, 21:31-32)

â€¢ ••Matthew's Decision to Follow Jesus••
	• Matthew opened his heart to Jesus Christ and became a new person
	• This was not an easy decision, as he lost income and faced persecution from his old friends

â€¢ ••Matthew's Hospitality••
	• Matthew opened his home to his old friends and invited them to meet Jesus
	• He gave a great feast and invited tax collectors and sinners, including possibly Gentiles

â€¢ ••Pharisaic Criticism••
	• The Pharisees criticized Jesus for eating with tax collectors and sinners
	• They tried to create a disagreement among the disciples of John the Baptist (Luke 5:33)

â€¢ ••Jesus' Response to Criticism••
	• Jesus explained that He came to call sinners, not the righteous (Matt. 9:13)
	• He came to call the Pharisees as well, as they were spiritually sick and needed a physician.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Matthew's Background••
	• Matthew was a publican (tax collector) before following Jesus
	• He brought his pen with him, and the Holy Spirit used him to write the Gospel of Matthew
	• He ministered in Palestine and made missionary journeys to the Jews dispersed among the Gentiles

â€¢ ••Matthew's Gospel••
	• Matthew's Gospel is associated with Persia, Ethiopia, and Syria
	• Some traditions associate him with Greece
	• The New Testament is silent on his life, but his gospel continues to minister to hearts

â€¢ ••The Birth of Jesus••
	• Matthew's Gospel begins with the birth of Jesus Christ
	• He presents four facts about the King: His human heredity, divine heredity, virgin birth, and miraculous conception

â€¢ ••Jesus' Human Heredity••
	• Matthew gives Jesus' human heredity through Joseph, His foster father
	• This genealogy shows that Jesus is a part of history and that all of Jewish history prepared the way for His birth
	• The genealogy includes references to four women from Old Testament history: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Bathsheba

â€¢ ••Jesus' Divine Heredity••
	• Matthew's genealogy omits some names to give a systematic summary of three periods in Israel's history
	• The numerical value of the Hebrew letters for "David" equals fourteen, which may have been a memory aid
	• Jesus' divine heredity is more important than His human heredity to establish His rights to David's throne

â€¢ ••The Virgin Birth••
	• Jesus was born of an earthly mother without the need of an earthly father
	• This is known as the doctrine of the virgin birth
	• Jesus' birth was different from that of any other Jewish boy named in the genealogy

â€¢ ••Jesus' Eternal Nature••
	• Jesus existed before Mary and Joseph or any of His earthly ancestors
	• If Jesus were conceived and born just like any other baby, He could not be God
	• The miracle of the Holy Spirit conceived Jesus in the womb of Mary

â€¢ ••The Importance of the Genealogy••
	• The genealogy shows that Jesus is a part of history and that all of Jewish history prepared the way for His birth
	• It illustrates God's wonderful grace in including women in the genealogy
	• The genealogy is a vital part of the gospel record

â€¢ ••The Significance of the Virgin Birth••
	• The virgin birth is necessary for Jesus to be God
	• It is a miracle of the Holy Spirit that conceived Jesus in the womb of Mary
	• The virgin birth is a unique aspect of Jesus' birth that sets Him apart from other human beings

â€¢ ••The Purpose of Matthew's Gospel••
	• Matthew's Gospel is written to establish Jesus' rights to David's throne
	• It presents Jesus as the King of the Jews and the Son of God
	• The gospel continues to minister to hearts wherever the Scriptures travel in this world.

â€¢ ••Mary's Virginity••
	• Mary was a virgin when Jesus was conceived (Luke 1:26-38)
	• Some have questioned whether Mary was a virgin, but the word "virgin" in Matthew 1:23 cannot be translated to "young woman"

â€¢ ••Jesus' Genealogy••
	• Jesus' genealogy is traced through David's family (Matthew 1, Luke 3)
	• Jesus is the only Jew who can prove His claims to the throne of David

â€¢ ••Betrothal and Marriage••
	• In Jewish culture, betrothal was equivalent to marriage, except the couple did not live together
	• If a betrothed woman became pregnant, it was considered adultery (Deut. 22:13-21)

â€¢ ••Joseph's Response••
	• Joseph did not punish or divorce Mary when he discovered she was pregnant
	• This fulfilled Isaiah 7:14

â€¢ ••Jesus' Names••
	• Jesus means "Savior" and comes from the Hebrew name Joshua
	• Christ means "anointed" or "Messiah"
	• Emmanuel means "God with us"

â€¢ ••The Magi••
	• The magi were a group of scholars who studied the stars (astrologers)
	• They were given a special sign, a miraculous star, to announce the birth of the King

â€¢ ••The Magi's Journey••
	• The magi traveled from the East to Jerusalem, where they were told the King would be born in Bethlehem
	• They worshipped the Christ Child in Bethlehem

â€¢ ••The Magi's Identity••
	• We do not know how many magi there were
	• They were Gentiles and wealthy scholars

â€¢ ••Herod's Response••
	• Herod was afraid of the King and wanted to destroy Him
	• He was a cruel and crafty man who permitted no one to interfere with his rule

â€¢ ••Herod's Character••
	• Herod was a ruthless murderer who had his own family members killed
	• He was married at least nine times to fulfill his lusts and strengthen his political ties

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Herod's Motivation••
	• Herod wanted to kill Jesus to maintain his title as "King of the Jews"
	• He was an Idumaean, a descendant of Esau, and not a full-blooded Jew

â€¢ ••The Magi's Quest••
	• The magi were seeking the King, Jesus
	• They were Gentiles who sought and found Jesus, but the Jewish priests did not

â€¢ ••The Jewish Priests' Response••
	• They knew the Scriptures and pointed others to the Savior
	• But they did not go to worship Jesus themselves

â€¢ ••The Miraculous Star••
	• The star was not always visible to the magi
	• It led them to the house where Jesus was, after they had started their journey

â€¢ ••Prophecies Fulfilled••
	• Jesus' birth was a fulfillment of prophecy (Micah 5:2)
	• Jesus' birthplace, Bethlehem, was a fulfillment of prophecy (Bethlehem means "house of bread")

â€¢ ••Hostility against the King••
	• Herod pretended to worship Jesus, but actually wanted to destroy Him
	• God warned Joseph to take the child and Mary and flee to Egypt

â€¢ ••The Massacre of the Innocents••
	• Herod ordered the killing of boy babies two years of age and under in Bethlehem
	• This event was a fulfillment of prophecy (Jeremiah 31:15)

â€¢ ••The Significance of Bethlehem••
	• Bethlehem was associated with David, a type of Jesus Christ in His suffering and glory
	• The name Bethlehem means "house of bread", which relates to Jesus as the "Bread of Life"

â€¢ ••The Theme of Hostility••
	• Matthew introduced the theme of hostility, which he focused on throughout his book
	• Satan is a liar and a murderer, as was King Herod

â€¢ ••Prophecy and Fulfillment••
	• Jeremiah's prophecy about Rachel weeping for her children was fulfilled in the massacre of the innocents
	• This event was a reminder of Jacob's sorrow when Rachel died, and the mothers of Israel weeping for their sons going into captivity.

â€¢ ••The Significance of Bethlehem••

â€¢ ••The Restoration of Israel••

â€¢ ••The Call of Jesus••
	• Jesus was in Egypt, just like Moses, and was called out to go to Israel
	• Both Jesus and Moses demonstrated courage in obeying God's call

â€¢ ••The Reign of Archelaus••
	• Herod died in 4 BC, and Archelaus was crowned king, but the Jews protested his rule
	• Augustus Caesar agreed with the Jews and made Archelaus an ethnarch over half of his father's kingdom

â€¢ ••God's Leading••
	• Joseph and his family knew they were no safer under Archelaus than under Herod the Great
	• They prayed, waited, and sought God's will, demonstrating faith and trust in God's leading

â€¢ ••The Fulfillment of Prophecy••
	• Matthew points out that every detail in Jesus' life was foretold in the Scriptures
	• The term "Nazarene" was applied to Jesus and His followers, and may have been a reference to the Hebrew word "netzer," meaning "a branch or shoot"

â€¢ ••The Spiritual Connection••
	• The term "Nazarene" may have been a reference to Jesus' role as a branch or shoot of God's people
	• Several prophets apply this title to Jesus, emphasizing His role as a spiritual leader

â€¢ ••The Identity of Jesus••
	• Jesus grew up in Nazareth and was identified with that city
	• His enemies thought He had been born there, but He was actually born in Bethlehem

â€¢ ••The Power of the Holy Spirit and the Word of God••
	• Jesus was tempted by Satan in the wilderness (Matt. 4:1)
	• The power of the Holy Spirit and the Word of God are essential for overcoming temptation

â€¢ ••The Nature of Temptation••
	• Temptation involves the will and involves making choices that go against God's will
	• Jesus came to do the Father's will (Heb. 10:1-9)

â€¢ ••The First Temptation••
	• Satan tempted Jesus to use His divine powers to meet His own needs (Matt. 4:1-4)
	• Jesus quoted Deuteronomy 8:3 to defeat Satan, emphasizing the importance of feeding on and obeying God's Word

â€¢ ••The Second Temptation••
	• Satan quoted Psalm 91:11-12 to tempt Jesus to test God's care (Matt. 4:5-7)
	• Jesus replied with Deuteronomy 6:16, emphasizing the importance of not tempting God

â€¢ ••The Importance of Context••
	• Satan omitted the phrase "in all thy ways" when quoting Psalm 91
	• We must always compare spiritual things with spiritual (1 Cor. 2:13)

â€¢ ••The Dangers of Isolating Scripture••
	• Satan had cleverly isolated a text from its context to make a false point
	• We can prove almost anything by the Bible if we isolate texts from their contexts

â€¢ ••The Third Temptation••
	• Satan offered Jesus a shortcut to His kingdom (Matt. 4:8-11)
	• Jesus knew that He would suffer and die before entering into His glory (Luke 24:26; 1 Peter 1:11; 5:1)

â€¢ ••The Lie of Worshiping the Creature••
	• Satan has always wanted worship and to be God (Isa. 14:12-14)
	• Worshipping the creature instead of the Creator is a lie that rules our world today (Rom. 1:24-25)

â€¢ ••The Importance of Sharing in Suffering••
	• There are no shortcuts to the will of God (1 Peter 5:10)
	• If we want to share in the glory, we must also share in the suffering

â€¢ ••The Promise of the Kingdom••
	• The Father had already promised Jesus the kingdom (Ps. 2:8)
	• Jesus replied with Deuteronomy 6:13, emphasizing the importance of worshiping and serving the Lord alone

â€¢ ••Jesus' Victory over Satan••
	• Jesus defeated Satan in the wilderness
	• Satan continued to tempt Jesus, but Jesus remained victorious
	• Each victory over Satan does not guarantee freedom from further temptation

â€¢ ••The Order of the Temptations••
	• Luke's account of the temptations reverses the order of the second and third temptations as recorded in Matthew
	• Matthew's account follows the historical order, with Jesus' command to Satan at the end of the third temptation serving as proof

â€¢ ••Jesus' Ministry Begins••
	• After defeating Satan, Jesus was ready to begin His ministry
	• No one has the right to call others to obey who has not obeyed themselves

â€¢ ••Christ's Ministry of Power••
	• Matthew shows that every detail of Jesus' life was controlled by the Word of God
	• The ministry described in John 1:19-3:36 occurred between Jesus' temptation and the statement in Matthew 4:12

â€¢ ••The Light of Jesus••
	• Jesus brought the Light to people who were walking in darkness
	• He made His headquarters in Capernaum, a city in Galilee with a mixed population

â€¢ ••Jesus' Methods of Ministry••
	• Jesus brought the Light to Galilee through His teaching, preaching, and healing
	• He healed all manner of sickness and disease, with no case too difficult for Him

â€¢ ••The Result of Jesus' Ministry••
	• Jesus' miracles brought tremendous fame and a great following of people from many areas
	• News of His healing spread quickly, and people brought their afflicted friends and family members to Him

â€¢ ••The Types of Cases Jesus Healed••
	• Jesus healed diseases, torments, and people afflicted with demons
	• He also healed people with epilepsy (referred to as "lunatic") and paralysis (referred to as "palsy")

â€¢ ••The Scope of Jesus' Ministry••
	• Jesus' miracles of healing were just a part of His ministry throughout Galilee
	• He also taught and preached the Word, announcing it as a herald

â€¢ ••The Significance of Jesus' Ministry••

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••The Sermon on the Mount••
	• Jesus gave this message to individual believers, not to the unsaved world at large
	• The sermon has definite applications for us today
	• Jesus originally gave these words to His disciples (Matt. 5:1)
• ••True Righteousness••
	• Jesus described Christian character that flows from within
	• Righteousness is not just about obeying rules and regulations, but about having a right heart
• ••The Beatitudes••
	• Describe the attitudes that ought to be in our lives today
	• Four attitudes are described:
		- Attitude toward ourselves (v. 3): humility and honesty with ourselves
		- Attitude toward our sins (vv. 4-6): mourning over sin and seeking to treat it the way God does
		- Attitude toward the Lord (vv. 7-9): experiencing God's mercy and sharing it with others
		- Attitude toward the world (vv. 10-16): being a peacemaker and a channel for God's mercy and peace
• ••Character vs. Conduct••
	• Conduct flows out of character
	• The Pharisees were concerned about minute details of conduct, but neglected the major matter of character
• ••The Meaning of "Blessed"••
	• The word "blessed" means "divine joy and perfect happiness"
	• It implies an inner satisfaction and sufficiency that does not depend on outward circumstances
• ••Meekness••
	• Meekness is not weakness, but power under control
	• It refers to a horse that has been broken, and is used to describe a person who has been broken and humbled
• ••The World's Attitude vs. God's Attitude••
	• The world praises pride, not humility
	• The world endorses sin, especially if you "get away with it"
	• The world is at war with God, while God is seeking to reconcile His enemies
• ••The Christian's Attitude••
	• Christians should have a radically different outlook from the world
	• We should seek to be humble, honest, and meek, and to share God's mercy and peace with others
• ••The Christian's Relationship with the World••
	• There is conflict between Christians and the world
	• We are different from the world and have different attitudes
	• We should seek to be peacemakers and channels for God's mercy and peace in a troubled world

â€¢ ••Little Faith - Misunderstanding Christ (16:5-12)••

â€¢ ••Jesus' teachings are often misunderstood••

â€¢ ••The Law of Moses on Divorce••
	• The law in Deuteronomy 24:1-4 allowed men to divorce their wives, but not women to divorce their husbands.
	• The official "bill of divorce" was given to the wife to declare her status and allow her to remarry.

â€¢ ••Grounds for Divorce••
	• The law did not specify adultery as grounds for divorce, as adulterers and adulteresses were stoned to death.
	• The phrase "some uncleanness" in Deuteronomy 24:1 is unclear, but it was not adultery.

â€¢ ••Jesus' Explanation••
	• Jesus said Moses gave the divorce law because of the sinfulness of the human heart.
	• The law protected the wife by restraining the husband from impulsively divorcing her.

â€¢ ••God's Intentions••
	• God was not putting His approval on divorce or encouraging it.
	• He was seeking to restrain it and make it more difficult for men to dismiss their wives.

â€¢ ••The Original Creation••
	• God established marriage in the beginning (Genesis 1:27; 2:21-25).
	• Marriage is a sacred and permanent union between a man and a woman.

â€¢ ••The Nature of Marriage••
	• Marriage is a physical union, not a spiritual one.
	• The two become one flesh, not one spirit.

â€¢ ••Breaking the Marriage Union••
	• Only a physical cause can break the marriage union: death or fornication.
	• The "exception clause" in Matthew 5:32 and 19:9 allows for divorce in cases of fornication.

â€¢ ••Remarriage after Divorce••
	• Remarriage after divorce, except in cases of fornication, makes the person guilty of committing adultery.
	• Jesus included women in His warning, elevating their status in society.

â€¢ ••God's Authority••
	• God has the right to lay down the rules for marriage.
	• A divorce may be legal according to human laws, but not right in God's eyes.

â€¢ ••Commitment in Marriage••
	• God expects married people to practice commitment to each other.
	• Marriage is a lifelong commitment, and divorce should not be viewed as an easy way out.

••1. The Signs of the Times••
• The signs of the times are a warning to believers to be prepared for increasing opposition and persecution (Mark 13:9-13)
• Believers are to take heed to themselves and not be discouraged by the challenges ahead

••2. Opposition and Persecution••
• Opposition and persecution will come from both official and personal sources (Mark 13:9-13)
• Believers will face persecution in local Jewish courts and higher courts involving governors and kings

••3. Witnessing in the Midst of Persecution••
• Persecution will only result in proclamation of the gospel (Mark 13:10)
• Believers will suffer for Jesus' sake and declare His gospel through their witness

••4. The Commission to Witness••
• Jesus' commission to His people is to take the gospel to all nations (Matthew 28:19-20)
• This commission is not a condition for Jesus' return, but a command to His people

••5. The Holy Spirit's Ministry••
• The Holy Spirit will minister through believers whenever they have opportunity to witness (Mark 13:11)
• This passage is an encouragement for all believers who sincerely want to witness for Christ

••6. Personal Persecution••
• Friends and family members may create problems for believers due to their loyalty to their "ancient faith" and nation (Micah 7:4ff; John 15:18-27)
• The Christian faith was looked on as heresy and blasphemy by both Jews and Gentiles

••7. The Real Cause of Persecution••
• The real cause of persecution is stated in Mark 13:13: "for my name's sake"
• If we identify with Jesus Christ, we can expect the world to treat us the way it treated Him (John 15:20ff)

••8. Salvation and Persecution••
• Mark 13:13 is not a condition for salvation, but applies primarily to witnesses during the tribulation
• True believers will prove their faith by their faithfulness during the tribulation (Revelation 13)

••9. The Abomination of Desolation••
• The phrase "abomination of desolation" comes from the book of Daniel and refers to the idolatrous pollution of the Jewish temple
• The Jewish temple was defiled in 167 BC by the Syrian king Antiochus IV and again in AD 70 by the Romans

••10. The Middle of the Tribulation••
• The middle of the tribulation is marked by the abomination of desolation (Mark 13:14-18)
• This event is a fulfillment of Daniel 11:31 and a warning to believers to be prepared for the challenges ahead.

	• They developed out of the ministry of Ezra, who taught the Jewish people to obey the law of Moses
	• However, the movement became legalistic and hypocritical over time
• ••Jesus Heals a Man with Palsy••

	• Jesus not only healed the man's body but also forgave his sins
• ••The Faith of the Man's Friends••
	• The man's four friends had faith that Jesus would heal him
	• Their love for the man united them in their efforts to get him to Jesus
	• They were willing to go to great lengths to help their friend, even removing tiles from the roof
• ••Jesus Teaches a Lesson about Sin and Forgiveness••
	• Jesus used the opportunity to teach a lesson about sin and forgiveness
	• He healed the man's body, which was a visible evidence of the spiritual healing within
	• The healing was a demonstration of Jesus' authority to forgive sins
• ••The Scribes and Pharisees React••
	• The scribes and Pharisees were astonished by Jesus' claim to have authority to forgive sins
	• They considered this claim to be blasphemy, as only God can forgive sins
	• They could not deny the miracle of healing, but they rejected Jesus' claim to forgive sins
• ••The Significance of the Title "Son of Man"••
	• The title "Son of Man" was first used in Luke's gospel in Luke 5:24
	• It was a title that was familiar to Jesus' listeners, who had heard it used of the prophet Ezekiel and Daniel
	• The title would be used 23 times in Luke's gospel
• ••Jesus' Claim to Forgiveness••

	• This claim was a demonstration of Jesus' divinity
	• The scribes and Pharisees rejected this claim, but it was a key aspect of Jesus' ministry
• ••The Importance of Faith and Love••

	• Their love for the man united them in their efforts to help him
	• This story highlights the importance of faith and love in the Christian life
• ••The Miraculous Healing••
	• The healing of the man with palsy was a miraculous demonstration of God's power

	• The healing was a key aspect of Jesus' ministry, demonstrating his authority to forgive sins.

• ••Jesus' Teaching on Generosity••
	• Jesus taught that the poor and handicapped should be given priority at public banquets.
	• This is because they cannot pay us back, and our hearts should be motivated by a desire to serve others.
	• When we serve others from an unselfish heart, we are laying up treasures in heaven (Matt. 6:20).
• ••The Dangers of Selfishness••
	• In a competitive world, it's easy for God's people to become more concerned with profit and loss than with sacrifice and service.
	• We must strive to maintain an unselfish attitude, as Jesus had, and share what we have with others.
• ••The Jews' False Security••
	• The Jewish people pictured their future kingdom as a great feast with Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the prophets as honored guests.
	• One guest was confident that he would be at the "kingdom feast" with them, but Jesus told a parable that revealed the sad consequences of false confidence.
• ••The Parable of the Great Feast••
	• A host invited guests to a dinner, but they all refused to attend, giving feeble excuses.
	• The first guest had purchased a piece of land and wanted to examine it first.
	• The second guest had purchased ten oxen and wanted to test them.
	• The third guest had gotten married and didn't want to leave his new wife.
• ••The Excuses of the Guests••
	• The guests' excuses were weak and showed that they were not truly committed to attending the feast.
	• They expected to get another invitation in the future, but that invitation never came.
• ••The Host's Disappointment••
	• The host had prepared a great dinner for many guests, but they all refused to attend.
	• The host was disappointed and frustrated by the guests' lack of commitment.
• ••The Importance of Commitment••
	• When we make commitments, we should follow through on them.
	• We should not make excuses or expect to get another chance.
• ••The Consequences of False Confidence••
	• The guests in the parable were confident that they would get another invitation, but that invitation never came.
	• This shows the sad consequences of false confidence and the importance of being committed to our commitments.
• ••The Need for Humility••
	• We should be humble and recognize that we are not guaranteed a place at the "kingdom feast".
	• We should strive to be committed and faithful, rather than relying on false confidence.

••1. Jesus' Return and Judgment••
• Jesus will return to judge His enemies

••2. Separation of the Saved and Lost••
• The image of eagles and vultures gathering at a corpse parallels the separation of the saved and lost
• The description in Revelation 19:17-21 also parallels the image of carrion-eating birds feasting on flesh

••3. Importance of Being Ready••
• The primary interpretation of these verses is for Israel in the end times, but they also emphasize the importance of being ready for the church
• Christians must not be like Lot's wife, who looked back in spite of the angels' warning

• The only way to save one's life is to lose it for the sake of Christ and the gospel

••5. Civilization as a "Rotting Corpse"••

• Dr. Luke wrote about various characters, including widows and politicians, Pharisees and publicans, little children and adults, rich men and beggars

••8. The Demanding Widow••
• Luke mentions widows more than any other gospel writer combined
• The early church was serious about caring for Christian widows, as seen in Acts 6:1 and 1 Timothy 5:3-10

••9. The Eastern Setting of the Courtroom••
• The "courtroom" was not a fine building but a tent that was moved from place to place
• The judge, not the law, set the agenda, and he sat regally in the tent surrounded by his assistants

••10. Overcoming Obstacles as a Widow••
• The widow had three obstacles to overcome: being a woman, having little standing before the law, and needing to bribe an assistant to have her case tried
• The story of the demanding widow teaches us about perseverance and faith in the face of adversity.

	• He was slain on Passover as the sacrifice for the world's sins (1 Cor. 5:7)

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Celebration of the Passover••
	• The theme of the celebration was peace
	• The leaders knew they had to act against Jesus
	• Judas' cooperation solved their problem

â€¢ ••The Theme of Peace••
	• The theme was "peace in heaven" instead of "peace on earth"
	• Jesus' work on the cross brought peace with God
	• The appeal is to be reconciled to God

â€¢ ••Jesus' Lamentation••
	• Jesus wept openly, like the prophet Jeremiah
	• He wept over the destruction of Jerusalem
	• He saw spiritual ignorance and blindness in the people

â€¢ ••The Cause of Jesus' Weeping••
	• The nation had wasted its opportunities
	• The people were ignorant of their "time of visitation"
	• The temple had become a den of thieves

â€¢ ••The Temple's Corruption••
	• The temple was a place of religious activity with little spiritual value
	• The priests were using the temple for personal gain
	• The court of the Gentiles was used for a "religious marketplace"

â€¢ ••Jesus' Cleansing of the Temple••
	• Jesus cursed the fig tree and cleansed the temple for the second time
	• He used the temple as a gathering place for those in need
	• He healed many who were sick and afflicted

â€¢ ••The Judgment of Jerusalem••
	• Jesus wept over the terrible judgment that was coming to the nation
	• The Romans would destroy the city and temple in AD 70
	• The people did not know that God had visited them

â€¢ ••The People's Rejection of Jesus••
	• The people did not recognize Jesus as the Messiah
	• They said, "We will not have this man to reign over us"
	• They rejected Jesus, just like the nation of Israel

â€¢ ••The Priests' Corruption••
	• The priests were preying on the people instead of praying for them
	• They were using the temple for personal gain
	• They were hiding their sins behind the temple's services

â€¢ ••Jesus' Ministry in the Temple••
	• Jesus used the temple as a gathering place for those in need
	• He healed many who were sick and afflicted
	• He taught and ministered to those who were seeking God

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••Jesus' Courage and Purpose••
	• Jesus had set His face like a flint to go to Jerusalem
	• He would face His enemies and go to the cross to die for the sins of the world
	• He still summons us to be courageous
• ••The Conflict with Religious Leaders••
	• Jesus had already told the Twelve to expect conflict and suffering in Jerusalem
	• The chief priests, scribes, and elders challenged Jesus because He had cleansed the temple and called them "thieves"
	• They tried to catch Him in His words to arrest Him as an enemy of the state
• ••The Examination of Jesus••
	• Jesus was watched and tested by His enemies during His final week
	• Despite what they saw and learned, they rejected Him
	• However, Jesus was also examining them, revealing their ignorance, hatred, and unbelief
• ••The Question about Authority••
	• The chief priests, scribes, and elders asked Jesus what authority He had to cleanse the temple
	• They claimed their authority from Moses, the law, and the rabbis
	• Jesus turned the question around and put them on the defensive
• ••Jesus' Wise Approach••
	• He asked a question, gave a parable, and quoted a prophecy to reveal the sins of the nation of Israel
	• He revealed their past rejection of John the Baptist, who had pointed to Jesus
• ••The Sin of Rejection••
	• The Jews had carefully examined the Passover lambs for blemishes, but rejected Jesus despite His purity
	• Jesus was the Lamb of God, but they rejected Him
• ••The Examination of the Nation••
	• Jesus questioned the chief priests, scribes, and elders, revealing their ignorance, hatred, and unbelief
	• Their responses showed their hearts were far from God
• ••The Importance of Authority••
	• Authority is essential for the success of any social, political, or religious organization
	• Without authority, there is confusion and chaos
• ••The Confrontation with Jesus••
	• The chief priests, scribes, and elders wanted to push Jesus into a dilemma to arrest Him
	• However, Jesus was not afraid and turned the question around to reveal their sins
• ••The Significance of the Event••
	• The confrontation with Jesus was a dramatic event that captured the attention of the people
	• It revealed the sins of the nation of Israel and the rejection of Jesus, the Lamb of God

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Parable of the Vineyard••
	• Jesus tells a parable about a vineyard owner who sends servants to collect fruit, but they are rejected and beaten.
	• The parable is about the Jewish leaders' rejection of God's messengers and their ultimate rejection of Jesus.

â€¢ ••The Jewish Leaders' Dilemma••
	• The Jewish leaders are in a dilemma because they know they will be punished no matter what they do.
	• They decide to "play dumb" and not answer Jesus' question, showing their deceitfulness.

â€¢ ••Their Present Rebellion••
	• The Jewish leaders have disobeyed God's message through John the Baptist and will continue to disobey Jesus' message.
	• They have rejected God's blessings and have refused to obey His statutes.

â€¢ ••God's Patience and Judgment••
	• God has been patient with the Jewish leaders, sending one servant after another, but they have refused to obey.
	• They have finally rejected Jesus, God's beloved Son, and will be judged for their actions.

â€¢ ••The Parable's Meaning••
	• The parable illustrates the Jewish leaders' thinking: if they kill the son, they can claim the vineyard for themselves.
	• This is similar to the Sanhedrin's thinking when they condemned Jesus to death.

â€¢ ••The Messiah and the Stone••
	• Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22, claiming to be the Messiah and the "stone" that the builders rejected.
	• The "stone" is a symbol of God and the promised Messiah, and those who trust Jesus find Him to be the foundation stone and chief cornerstone.

â€¢ ••The Warning to the Sanhedrin••
	• Jesus warns the Sanhedrin that they will only destroy themselves if they condemn Him.
	• This principle applies today, and unbelievers should heed Jesus' warning.

â€¢ ••The Unpardonable Sin••
	• The Jewish leaders have committed the unpardonable sin by rejecting the witness of the Holy Spirit through the apostles.
	• This sin is evidenced by the stoning of Stephen, after which the gospel went from the Jews to the Samaritans and then to the Gentiles.

â€¢ ••The Insidious Nature of Sin••
	• The parable illustrates the insidious nature of sin: the more we sin, the worse it becomes.
	• The tenants started off beating servants and ended up becoming murderers.

â€¢ ••The Consequences of Rejection••
	• The Jewish leaders' rejection of Jesus will lead to their ruin and judgment.
	• This principle applies today, and those who reject Jesus will face the consequences of their actions.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••God's Witness to the World••
	• God's witness to the world is ended when people reject His message and messengers (John 12:35-43, Heb. 2:1-4)
	• Rejection of God's message is a serious thing

â€¢ ••Question about Caesar••
	• Jesus was questioned by spies sent by the Pharisees and Herodians about taxes and Roman authority
	• Jesus lifted the discussion to a higher level, discussing the relationship between the kingdom of God and human governments

â€¢ ••Governmental Authority••

	• Christians should obey earthly authorities for the Lord's sake, but put God first when obedience to God conflicts with obedience to man

â€¢ ••Citizenship and Responsibility••
	• As citizens of heaven, Christians are strangers and pilgrims on earth, but should not ignore their earthly responsibilities
	• Human government is essential to a safe and orderly society

â€¢ ••Respecting Authority••
	• Even if we cannot respect the people in office, we must respect the office
	• We should seek to be good citizens and honor God in our relationships with earthly authorities

â€¢ ••The Image of God••
	• God's image is stamped on us, and He has the right to command our lives as citizens in His kingdom
	• We should seek to be good citizens and glorify God in our relationships with earthly authorities

â€¢ ••The Misconception of Obnoxious Behavior••
	• Some Christians mistakenly believe that being obnoxious as citizens pleases God and witnesses for Christ
	• We should seek to be peacemakers and not troublemakers

â€¢ ••The Example of Daniel••
	• Daniel is an example of a good citizen who honored God in his relationships with earthly authorities (Dan. 1)

â€¢ ••The Question about Moses••
	• The Sadducees asked Jesus a hypothetical question about levirate marriage, which they claimed was not addressed in the Jewish law
	• Jesus pointed out that their question revealed assumptions that limited God's power and denied God's Word

â€¢ ••The Resurrection••
	• Resurrection is not reconstruction, but the miraculous granting of a new body that has continuity with the old body but not identity
	• Jesus' resurrection body was the same as before His death and yet different, demonstrating the power of God to grant new life.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••The Future Life with God••
	• Will not be a continuation of the present life on a higher scale
	• We will maintain our identities and know each other
	• There will be no more death, hence no need for marriage and procreation

â€¢ ••Angels and Humanity••
	• Angels appear in Scripture as men, but are spirit beings without sexuality
	• We will be like them in heaven, with no marriage or childbearing

â€¢ ••The Power of God••
	• God is powerful enough to raise the dead and give them new bodies
	• He can give different bodies to various things in creation, so why not to people?

â€¢ ••The Sadducees' Mistake••
	• They denied the power of God in their attempt to be rational
	• Jesus referred them to the Word of God, particularly Exodus 3

â€¢ ••The Reality of Life After Death••
	• God is the God of the whole person - spirit, soul, and body
	• He will not keep us disembodied spirits forever, but will give us glorious bodies

â€¢ ••God's Covenantal Relationship••
	• He made promises of earthly blessing to the patriarchs and their descendants
	• He cannot fulfill these promises if His people are going to live forever only as disembodied spirits

â€¢ ••Jesus' Affirmation••
	• He affirmed the existence of angels, life after death, and the hope of a future resurrection
	• He did it with only one passage from Moses, Exodus 3

â€¢ ••The Question about David••
	• Jesus asked the Pharisees a final question: "What do you think about the Christ?"
	• Their answer was based on their understanding of the Messiah as the Son of David

â€¢ ••The Enigma of Psalm 110••
	• The Jewish religious leaders identified Psalm 110 as a prophetic psalm
	• The psalm presents an enigma: how can the Messiah be both David's Lord and his son?

â€¢ ••The Explanation••
	• The only explanation is that the Messiah must be both God and man
	• As eternal God, He is David's Lord, but as man, He is David's son

â€¢ ••The Need for Discernment••

	• The shepherd would guard the flock at night, lying across the opening
	• In the morning, the shepherds would come, call their sheep, and assemble their own flocks
• ••The True Shepherd••
	• The true shepherd comes in through the door, recognized by the porter
	• The thieves and robbers cannot enter through the door, but must climb over the wall and deceive the sheep
	• The sheep follow only the voice of their own shepherd
• ••The False Shepherds••
	• The false shepherds are those who lead the sheep astray, but cannot follow them
	• They must steal the sheep away, as they cannot lead them
• ••The Purpose of Jesus' Teaching••
	• Jesus' teaching is not a parable, but a dark saying or proverb
	• The occasion for this lesson was the excommunication of the beggar from the synagogue
• ••The Identity of the Sheepfold••
	• The sheepfold is not heaven, but the nation of Israel
	• The Gentiles are the "other sheep" not of the fold of Israel
• ••Jesus' Role as the Shepherd••
	• Jesus came to the nation of Israel, the appointed way
	• He came to take in those who were mistreated and excluded, like the beggar
• ••The Importance of Jesus' Teaching••
	• The teaching in John 10 is important for understanding who Jesus is and what He wants to do for us
	• The symbols used by Jesus help us understand spiritual truths
• ••Misinterpretations of John 10:1••
	• The verse is often used to teach that those who try to get into heaven by any means other than Christ will fail
	• However, this is not based on the verse, and Jesus made it clear that the fold is the nation of Israel

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction••

• The gospel is a message of power that can be taken to all people
	• It's a message of salvation that's suitable for everyone, regardless of their need or station in life
	• Faith in Christ is what saves the sinner, not behavior

••II. The Theme of Romans••

• The key verse of the letter is Romans 1:17, which announces the theme: "the righteousness of God"
	• The word "righteousness" is used over 60 times in the letter
	• God's righteousness is revealed in the gospel through the death and resurrection of Christ

••III. The Problem of Sin••

• The problem of how a holy God can forgive sinners and still be holy is answered in the gospel
	• Through the death and resurrection of Christ, God is seen to be "both just and justifier" (Rom. 3:26)

••IV. The Gospel Reveals a Righteousness by Faith••

• In the Old Testament, righteousness was by works, but sinners couldn't obey God's law
	• Paul refers to Habakkuk 2:4, which says "The just shall live by his faith"
	• This verse is quoted three times in the New Testament: Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11, and Hebrews 10:38

••V. The Courtroom of Romans••

• When you study Romans, you walk into a courtroom where Paul defends God's salvation
	• He explains how the Christian can experience victory, liberty, and security through justification by faith

••VI. Chapters 9-11••

• These chapters are not a parenthesis or a detour, but a complete history of Israel, past, present, and future
	• Paul explains how God's righteousness relates to Israel in the new age of the church

••VII. The Practical Outworking of God's Righteousness••

• The practical outworking of God's righteousness in the life of the believer begins with dedication to God (Rom. 12:1-2)
	• Continues with ministry in the church (Rom. 12:3-21)
	• Then obedience to the government (Rom. 13:1-14)

••VIII. Living Right••

• The book of Romans is saying to us: "Be right!" Be right with God, with yourself, and with others
	• The righteousness of God received by faith makes it possible for us to live right lives

••IX. The Need for Righteousness••

• Rome needed this message, and we need it today: "Be right!"
	• The book of Romans is a call to righteousness, not just for individuals, but for society as a whole

••X. The Courtroom of God••

• The book of Romans is like a courtroom where God makes three declarations that prove all men are sinners and need Jesus Christ
	• The Gentile world is guilty (Rom. 1:18-32)
	• The Jewish world is guilty (Rom. 2:1-29)
	• All men are guilty and need salvation (Rom. 3:1-20)

• ••Devolution of Man••

• ••Intelligence (vv. 18-20)••
	• Man knew God through creation and the things He made
	• Man suppressed God's truth to live his own life and not be convicted by God's truth
	• Man turned truth into lies and became like a beast in thinking and living

	• Man's empty mind and darkened heart led to foolishness and idolatry
	• Man became a philosopher, but his wisdom only revealed his foolishness
• ••Idolatry••
	• Man exchanged the glory of the true God for substitute gods he made
	• Man's first false god was himself, fulfilling Satan's purpose in Genesis 3:5
	• Man descended to worshiping birds, beasts, and bugs
• ••Indulgence (vv. 24-27)••
	• Man's idolatry led to immorality and self-indulgence
	• Man exchanged truth for "the lie" and abandoned truth completely
	• Man became his own god, worshiping and serving himself

â€¢ ••The Need for Sanctification••

â€¢ ••The Objections to Justification by Faith••

	• Objection 2: "If we are no longer under the law, then we are free to live as we please"
	• Objection 3: "You have made God's law sinful"

â€¢ ••The Importance of Sanctification••

â€¢ ••Understanding the Law and Grace••
	• Christians are saved by grace, not by keeping the law
	• Some people argue that if we're saved by grace, we're free to live as we please
	• Others argue that we must live under the law to please God

â€¢ ••The Problem of Legalism••
	• Legalism is the belief that we can become holy and please God by obeying laws
	• It measures spirituality by a list of dos and don'ts
	• It fails to understand the real purpose of God's law and the relationship between law and grace

		- The Relationship between Law and Sin (7:7-13)
		- The Relationship between Law and Grace (7:14-25)

â€¢ ••The Relationship between Law and Sin••

â€¢ ••The Relationship between Law and Grace••

â€¢ ••The Purpose of the Law••

	• The law is like a shadow, pointing us to the reality of Christ

	• The Christian is no longer under the law, but rather under grace
	• The law is not a means of salvation, but rather a guide for living

••10. The Importance of Humility••

	• In Eastern society at the time, women wore long hair and a covering over their heads as a symbol of submission and purity.
	• The head-covering was a way of showing respect for the traditional social norms and customs.
• ••God's Order in the Church••
	• Paul emphasized that God's order in the church is based on three fundamentals: redemption, headship, and submission.
	• The order of headship is: God the Father, Christ, man, and woman.
• ••The Meaning of Headship••
	• Headship does not mean inequality or inferiority, but rather a position of authority and responsibility.
	• The woman is subject to the man, but is equal to him in Christ.
• ••The Importance of Respecting Symbols of Headship••
	• Both women and men must honor the Lord by respecting the symbols of headship, including hair and head-coverings.
	• Women must have long hair and wear a covering, while men should have short hair and not wear a covering.
• ••The Corinthian Women's Mistake••
	• The Corinthian women who appeared in public without head-coverings were actually putting themselves on the same level as temple prostitutes.
	• This was seen as a challenge to the traditional social norms and customs of the time.
• ••The Purpose of Paul's Teaching••
	• Paul's teaching was not intended to restrict women's roles in the church, but rather to promote order and respect for the traditional social norms and customs.
	• His goal was to promote peace and harmony in the church.
• ••The Application of Paul's Teaching••
	• Paul's teaching on headship and submission is still relevant today, and is intended to promote respect and harmony in the church.
	• Both women and men must honor the Lord by respecting the symbols of headship and submitting to one another in love.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••1. Paul's Victory••
• Paul saw himself as a victorious general, having claimed the spoils of battle (lost souls) for Christ.
• Believers are like the victorious general's sons, following in Christ's triumph.

••2. Ministry as Incense••
• Paul compared the Christian ministry to incense, which has a different effect on different people.
• To God, believers are the fragrance of Jesus Christ.
• To believers, we are the fragrance of life.
• To unbelievers, we are the fragrance of death.

••3. Sufficiency in Ministry••
• Paul asked, "And who is sufficient for these things?" (2 Cor. 2:16).
• He answered that his sufficiency is of God (2 Cor. 3:5).
• He reminded the Corinthians that his heart was pure and his motives sincere.

••4. Overcoming Obstacles••
• Circumstances may discourage us, and people may oppose us and misunderstand us.
• But we have in Christ the spiritual resources to win the battle: a clear conscience, a compassionate heart, and a conquering faith.

••5. God's Victory••
• If God is for us, who can be against us? (Rom. 8:31).
• We are more than conquerors through him who loved us (Rom. 8:37).

••6. Counterfeit Gospel••
• A counterfeit "gospel" appeared, a mixture of law and grace, carried by the "Judaizers".
• They taught that salvation was by faith in Christ plus the keeping of the law.

••7. Paul's Refutation••
• Paul refuted the doctrines and practices of the legalistic false teachers by showing the surpassing glory of the ministry of the gospel of the grace of God.

••8. The Judaizers' Methods••
• Paul saw the Judaizers as "peddlers" of the Word of God, using devious methods to teach the Bible.
• They boasted about their converts and "robbed" the church.

••9. Paul's Ministry••
• Paul's ministry was characterized by sincerity and a pure heart.
• He did not need to be clever or "peddle" the Word of God, as he was following in the triumphant train of the victorious Savior.

••10. The Glory of the Gospel••
• The gospel of God's grace is a glorious ministry that surpasses the glory of the Old Covenant.
• Paul's ministry was a ministry of the new covenant, characterized by the glory of the gospel of the grace of God.

	• Paul circumcised Timothy, a part-Jew, to facilitate his ministry among the Jews
	• This was different from the case of Titus, a full Gentile, who did not need to be circumcised

	• Paul's view prevailed in the private and public meetings

â€¢ ••Paul's Philosophy of Ministry••

â€¢ ••The Enemies of Grace••

â€¢ ••The Importance of the Gospel••
	• The gospel of God's grace, centered in Jesus Christ, is the only true gospel

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••1. The Importance of Reaching God's Goal••
• The goal is not to be successful in the eyes of men, but to reach the goal God has established for us.
• We must "take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of [us]" (Phil. 3:12 NIV).

••2. The Need for Discipline••
• Discipline is essential in running the Christian race.
• We must obey the "spiritual rules" laid down in the Word (Phil. 3:15-16).

••3. The Consequences of Breaking the Rules••
• Breaking the rules can lead to disqualification and loss of rewards.
• Examples include Jim Thorpe, who lost his Olympic medals for breaking the rules.

••4. The Importance of Obedience••
• Obedience to the rules is essential in the Christian life.
• We must compete according to the rules to receive a prize (2 Tim. 2:5).

••5. The Judgment Seat of Christ••
• Each Christian will stand before the judgment seat of Christ (Rom. 14:10-12).
• The Greek word for "judgment seat" is bema, the same word used to describe the Olympic judges' platform.

••6. The Danger of Disregarding God's Rules••
• Many people in the Bible began the race with great success but failed at the end due to disregarding God's rules.
• Examples include Lot, Samson, Saul, and Ananias and Sapphira.

••7. The Excitement of Running the Christian Race••
• Running the Christian race daily, "looking unto Jesus" (Heb. 12:1-2), is an exciting experience.
• The prospect of standing before the bema to receive rewards motivates us.

••8. Paul's Motivation••
• Paul's motivation was the future prospect of standing before the bema to receive rewards.

••9. The Problem of Professed Christians••
• Some professed Christians were living in a way that was contrary to the gospel.
• Paul was heartbroken over this and wept for them.

••10. The Description of the Judaizers••
• The Judaizers were "enemies of the cross of Christ" who added the law of Moses to the work of redemption.
• They emphasized obedience to the Old Testament dietary laws and circumcision, making a "god" out of the belly.

• ••The Importance of the Epistle to the Colossians••
	• Written by Paul around AD 60

• ••The City of Colosse••
	• Located about 100 miles inland from Ephesus

	• Gradually declined in importance, becoming a small town
• ••The Church in Colosse••
	• Founded by laymen Epaphras and Philemon
	• Started as a result of Paul's ministry in Ephesus
	• Had a significant impact on the surrounding area
• ••The Founders of the Colossian Church••
	• Epaphras: shared the gospel with friends in Colosse and had a ministry in Hierapolis and Laodicea
	• Philemon: had a church meeting in his home and likely had a son, Archippus, who was the pastor
• ••The Significance of the Colossian Church••
	• Demonstrates that God can use laymen to start ministries
	• Shows that God's plan is for Christians in urban areas to reach out to smaller towns and share the gospel
• ••The Church's Predominantly Gentile Membership••
	• The sins Paul named in Colossians 3:5-9 were commonly associated with Gentile culture
	• The church's membership was likely influenced by the surrounding culture
• ••The Influence of Eastern Religions••
	• The Colossian church was likely influenced by Eastern philosophies and religions
	• Paul's epistle addresses the need for Christians to be grounded in their faith and not influenced by false teachings
• ••The Importance of Paul's Epistle••
	• Addresses contemporary issues and provides guidance for the Colossian church
	• Demonstrates the importance of Paul's ministry and the impact of his epistles on the early Christian church
• ••The Relationship between Diet and Spiritual Living••
	• Paul addresses the relationship between diet and spiritual living in Colossians 2:20-23
	• Emphasizes the importance of living a life that is pleasing to God, rather than being controlled by external rules and regulations
• ••The Need for Christians to be Grounded in their Faith••
	• Paul's epistle emphasizes the need for Christians to be grounded in their faith and not influenced by false teachings
	• Demonstrates the importance of a strong spiritual foundation in order to resist the influence of the surrounding culture.

• ••The Purpose of Paul's Letter••
	• Paul wrote to the Colossians to refute heretical teachings and establish the truth of the gospel
	• The church was about 5 years old when Paul wrote this letter
• ••The Crisis in Colosse••
	• A crisis had occurred that threatened to destroy the ministry of the church
	• Paul was a prisoner in Rome when he wrote the letter
• ••The Heresy in Colosse••
	• A combination of Eastern philosophy and Jewish legalism with elements of gnosticism
	• The heresy promised people a close union with God and spiritual perfection
• ••The Characteristics of the Heresy••
	• Promised a "spiritual perfection" through teachings and ceremonies
	• Claimed a "full knowledge" and spiritual depth only available to the initiated
	• Believed in a series of "emanations" from God to His creation
	• Held to a form of astrology, believing angelic beings ruled heavenly bodies
• ••The Philosophical Background••
	• Grew out of the philosophical question of why there is evil in the world if creation was made by a holy God
	• Led to the false conclusion that matter is evil
• ••The Jewish Legalism••
	• Believed the rite of circumcision was helpful in spiritual development
	• Taught that the Old Testament law, especially dietary laws, was useful in attaining spiritual perfection
• ••The Two Schools of Thought••
	• One school taught that rigid discipline and asceticism was the way to conquer evil matter
	• The other view taught that it was permissible to engage in all kinds of sin since matter is evil anyway
• ••The Heresy's Impact on the Church••
	• Created problems and invaded the church
	• Threatened the peace and purity of the Colossian church
• ••Paul's Response••
	• Wrote the letter to refute the heretical teachings and establish the truth of the gospel
	• Used Epaphras, a willing companion, to help him in Rome
• ••The Significance of the Letter••
	• Refutes the heretical teachings and establishes the truth of the gospel
	• Provides insight into the philosophical and theological debates of the time

	• Jesus must have the preeminence in all things, not just as part of a larger system or philosophy

	• Seared conscience (cauterized)

	• Personal life becomes wrong before doctrines are changed

••9. Denial of God's Word••
	• False teachers combine Jewish legalism with Eastern asceticism
	• Deny the sufficiency of Christ's work on the cross
	• Promote their own teachings and traditions

••10. Warning to Believers••
	• Be aware of false teachers and their tactics
	• Recognize the signs of apostasy and hypocrisy

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••I. Introduction••

• The letter of Philemon is a short epistle written by Paul to his friend Philemon
	• Paul was a prisoner in Rome, while Philemon was in Colosse
	• The letter was carried to Colosse by Tychicus and Onesimus

••II. Paul's Greeting••

• Paul expresses his deep love for Philemon and the church in Colosse
	• He mentions that he is a prisoner for Jesus Christ
	• He includes Timothy in the greeting, but the burden of the letter is from Paul to Philemon

••III. Paul's Ministry••

• Paul's ministry was a "team" operation, involving his associates
	• He often included the names of his associates in his letters
	• He used the term "fellow worker" to describe his relationships with others

••IV. The Church in Colosse••

• The church in Colosse met in the home of Philemon and Apphia
	• Some people assume that Archippus was their son, but this is not certain
	• The church was founded as a result of Paul's ministry in Ephesus

••V. Onesimus's Conversion••

• Onesimus, a runaway slave, was converted by Paul in Rome
	• He had robbed his master and fled to Rome, but met Paul and was converted
	• Paul's conversion of Onesimus was a demonstration of God's providence

••VI. Paul's Appeal••

• Paul appeals to Philemon to forgive Onesimus and take him back as a brother
	• He reminds Philemon of his character and his love for Jesus Christ
	• He asks Philemon to consider the implications of forgiving Onesimus

••VII. Paul's Partnership••

• Paul reminds Philemon of their partnership in the gospel
	• He asks Philemon to consider his role in the church and his responsibilities to others
	• He reminds Philemon that he is a fellow worker in the gospel

••VIII. Paul's Confidence••

• Paul expresses his confidence in Philemon's response
	• He believes that Philemon will respond positively to his appeal
	• He is confident that Philemon will forgive Onesimus and take him back as a brother

••IX. Paul's Greetings••

• Paul greets Philemon and the church in Colosse
	• He sends greetings from Timothy and other associates
	• He expresses his love and appreciation for Philemon and the church

••X. The Significance of the Letter••

• The letter of Philemon is a beautiful example of God's providence
	• It demonstrates the power of forgiveness and the importance of relationships in the church
	• It shows that even in difficult circumstances, God can work out His plan for our lives.

â€¢ ••Jesus Christ's Unique Priesthood••

	• Faith is not just believing in spite of evidence, but obeying in spite of consequence.
	• Faith is confidence that God's Word is true and conviction that acting on that Word will bring His blessing.

â€¢ ••The Relationship Between Faith and Works••
	• James discussed the relationship between faith and works in James 2.
	• The discussion is important because it affects our eternal salvation.

â€¢ ••Three Kinds of Faith••
	• There are three kinds of faith: true saving faith, dead faith, and demonic faith.
	• Only true saving faith leads to salvation.

â€¢ ••Dead Faith••
	• Dead faith is a false declaration of faith that does not result in a changed life and good works.
	• People with dead faith substitute words for deeds and think that their words are as good as works.

â€¢ ••Characteristics of Dead Faith••
	• Dead faith is characterized by a lack of practical works.
	• People with dead faith may know the correct vocabulary for prayer and testimony, but their walk does not measure up to their talk.

â€¢ ••Illustration of Dead Faith••
	• James gave an illustration of a poor believer who came into a fellowship without proper clothing and in need of food.
	• The person with dead faith noticed the visitor's needs but did not do anything to meet them, only saying a few pious words.

â€¢ ••Obligation to Help Meet Needs••
	• As believers, we have an obligation to help meet the needs of people, no matter who they may be.
	• We should help those in need as an expression of love, and faith works by love.

â€¢ ••Consequences of Dead Faith••
	• Any declaration of faith that does not result in a changed life and good works is a false declaration.
	• The kind of faith that is never seen in practical works cannot save.

â€¢ ••Importance of Good Works••
	• Good works are an essential part of true saving faith.
	• We should not love with words or tongue but with actions and truth.

â€¢ ••Examples of Dead Faith••
	• The priest and Levite in the parable of the good Samaritan each had religious training but did not demonstrate their faith in loving works.
	• People with dead faith may quote the right verses from the Bible but do not live out their faith in practical works.

â€¢ ••Dead Faith••
	• Refers to faith that is only intellectual, without submission to God or trust in Christ

	• Is an illustration used by James to shock his complacent readers

	• They also recognize Jesus Christ as the Judge and submit to the power of His Word

â€¢ ••Comparison to Demonic Faith••
	• While demons believe and tremble, a person with dead faith is only touched in their intellect
	• A person can be enlightened in their mind and stirred in their heart, but still be lost forever

â€¢ ••True Saving Faith••
	• Involves a changed life, which can be seen and recognized
	• Is not just intellectual, but also emotional and practical
	• Results in good works, which are a natural outflow of faith

â€¢ ••Dynamic Faith••
	• Is the only kind of faith that can save the sinner
	• Is based on the Word of God, which is received and trusted
	• Results in a changed life, with good works that are a natural outflow of faith

â€¢ ••How to Show Faith without Works••

â€¢ ••The Power of God's Word••

	• It is not a process, but a once-for-all event that never changes
• ••A changed life is evidence of justification••
	• A person who is justified by faith will have a changed life and obey God's will
	• Their faith is demonstrated by their good works, which are a result of their obedience to God's will.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••1. Abraham's Faith and Works••
	• Abraham's obedience to God's command to sacrifice Isaac proved his faith (Gen. 22)
	• His faith and actions worked together, demonstrating a perfect relationship between faith and works (James 2:22)

••2. Justification by Faith and Works••
	• Abraham was justified by faith before God (Rom. 4)
	• He was justified by works before men, demonstrating his righteousness (James 2:21)

••3. Dynamic Faith••
	• Dynamic faith obeys God and proves itself in daily life and works (D.L. Moody's quote: "Every Bible should be bound in shoe leather")
	• It is not just intellectual assent, but a faith that acts on truth

••4. Rahab's Faith••
	• Rahab, a harlot, protected the Jewish spies and believed in God's promise to deliver the city of Jericho (Josh. 2)
	• Her faith was demonstrated by her actions, making her a great example of saving faith (Heb. 11:31)

••5. Rahab's Background••
	• Rahab ran a guest house and was an innkeeper (Josh. 2)
	• She was an immoral person, but became an ancestress of Jesus (Matt. 1:5)

••6. Types of Faith••
	• Dead faith: mere intellectual experience
	• Demonic faith: mind enlightened, emotions stirred, but no action
	• Dynamic faith: mind knows truth, heart is stirred, and will acts on truth

••7. Rahab's Faith in Action••
	• She risked her life to protect the spies and shared the good news with her family
	• Her faith was truly marvelous, considering the limited information she had

••8. Comparison with Unbelievers••
	• Rahab's faith is an indictment against unbelievers today, who have more information and revelation than she did
	• We have the full revelation of God through His Word and His Son, and the Holy Spirit to convict and teach us

••9. The Maturity of a Christian••
	• The mature Christian practices the truth in their daily life and works (James 2)
	• They do not just claim to know God, but demonstrate their faith through their actions

••10. The Importance of Works••
	• Works are not a means of salvation, but a demonstration of the faith that already exists
	• Faith and works are not separate, but intertwined, and demonstrate a perfect relationship between the two.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

â€¢ ••Peter's Background••
	• His given name was Simon, but Jesus changed it to Peter, meaning "a stone"
	• He was also known as Cephas in Aramaic
	• He was prone to failure as Simon, but Jesus made him a rock (Peter)

â€¢ ••Peter's Ministry••
	• He was one of the leading apostles in the early church, along with Paul
	• He was assigned to minister to the Jews, while Paul ministered to the Gentiles
	• He was commanded by Jesus to strengthen his brethren and tend the flock

â€¢ ••The Writing of 1 Peter••
	• The letter was written as a part of Peter's ministry to encourage and witness to his readers
	• It was not manufactured, but grew out of Peter's life lived to the glory of God
	• A number of events in Peter's life are woven into the fabric of the epistle

â€¢ ••Association with Silas••
	• Silas (also known as Silvanus) was a prophet and one of the "chief men" in the early church
	• He was associated with Peter's ministry and helped to lay the foundation of the church
	• He was originally part of Paul's team, but later worked with Peter

â€¢ ••Association with John Mark••
	• Peter mentioned John Mark in 1 Peter 5:13, who had failed on the mission field
	• Peter had led Mark to faith in Christ and maintained a concern for him
	• Paul later forgave and accepted Mark as a valued helper in the work

â€¢ ••The Location of the Church••
	• Peter indicated that he wrote the letter "at Babylon", which is likely a code name for Rome
	• There is no evidence that Peter ministered in ancient Babylon, but he may have ministered in Rome
	• Rome is called "Babylon" in Revelation 17:5 and 18:10

â€¢ ••Peter's Relationship with Paul••
	• Peter did not found the church in Rome nor serve as its first bishop
	• Paul would not have ministered in Rome had Peter arrived there first
	• Peter probably arrived in Rome after Paul was released from his first imprisonment, around AD 62

â€¢ ••The Recipients of the Letter••
	• Peter called them "strangers", meaning "resident aliens, sojourners"
	• They were citizens of heaven through faith in Christ and were not permanent residents on earth
	• They were like Abraham, with their eyes of faith centered on the future city of God

â€¢ ••The Purpose of the Letter••
	• The letter was written to encourage and witness to the readers
	• It was a personal letter, written out of Peter's life and experiences
	• It was not a manufactured letter, but grew out of Peter's ministry and life

â€¢ ••The Date and Circumstances of the Letter••
	• The letter was written around AD 63
	• Paul was martyred around the same time, and Peter may have laid down his life for Christ shortly after

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• ••The Audience of 1 Peter••
	• Christians who are considered "strangers" in the world (John 17:16)
	• "Scattered" people, meaning they lived outside of Palestine (diaspora)
	• A mixture of Jewish and Gentile Christians
• ••The Geographic Location••
	• Five different parts of the Roman Empire in northern Asia Minor (modern Turkey)
	• Possibly Jewish believers who had been under Peter's ministry migrated to these provinces
• ••The Purpose of the Letter••
	• To encourage believers to be good witnesses to their persecutors
	• To remind them that their suffering would lead to glory (1 Peter 1:6-7; 4:13-14; 5:10)
• ••The Suffering of Believers••
	• At least 15 times in the letter, Peter referred to suffering
	• Some suffered because they lived godly lives and did what was good and right (1 Peter 2:19-23; 3:14-18; 4:1-4, 15-19)
	• Others suffered reproach for the name of Christ (1 Peter 4:14) and were railed at by unsaved people (1 Peter 3:9-10)
• ••The Coming "Fiery Trial"••
	• Official persecution from the Roman Empire was about to begin
	• Peter knew that this trial was coming, and he wanted to prepare the churches
• ••The Events Leading Up to the Persecution••
	• Paul's defense of the Christian faith before the official court in Rome (Philippians 1:12-24)
	• Paul's martyrdom (2 Timothy 4:16-18)
	• Nero's persecution of Christians, including the blame for the fire of Rome (July AD 64)
• ••The Spread of Persecution••
	• Nero's persecution was local at first, but it probably spread
	• Other emperors followed Nero's example in later years
• ••The Help of 1 Peter••
	• Peter's letter was a tremendous help to Christians who suffered during the reigns of Trajan, Hadrian, and Diocletian
• ••The Variation of Suffering••
	• Suffering and opposition varied from place to place
	• Not all Christians in every part of the empire were going through the same trials to the same degree at the same time
• ••The Call to Persevere••
	• Peter encouraged believers to be good witnesses to their persecutors (1 Peter 3:9-10)
	• To remember that their suffering would lead to glory (1 Peter 1:6-7; 4:13-14; 5:10)

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

••1. Our security is not in ourselves, but in God's power••
	• Our faith in Christ unites us to Him, and His power guards and guides us.
	• We are not kept by our strength, but by God's faithfulness.

••2. We are guarded for glory••
	• We have already been glorified, and all that awaits is the public revelation of this glory.
	• God is so certain that we will be in heaven that He has already given us His glory as assurance.

••3. The assurance of heaven is a great help to us today••
	• Suffering today means glory tomorrow, making suffering a blessing to us.
	• The unsaved have their "glory" now, but it will be followed by eternal suffering.

••4. Christians are being prepared for glory••
	• God plans and performs all things here as preparation for what He has in store for us in heaven.
	• Life today is a school in which God trains us for our future ministry in eternity.

••5. Trials are a part of God's plan for us••
	• Trials are some of God's tools and textbooks in the school of Christian experience.
	• They meet our needs, discipline us, and prepare us for spiritual growth.

••6. Trials are varied and unpredictable••
	• Trials are manifold, meaning they come in many different forms and colors.
	• We must not think that because we have overcome one kind of trial, we will automatically "win them all."

••7. Trials are not easy••
	• Trials produce heaviness, or grief and pain.
	• To deny that our trials are painful is to make them even worse.

••8. Trials are controlled by God••
	• Trials do not last forever; they are "for a season."
	• God keeps His eye on the clock and His hand on the thermostat, and He will not permit us to suffer one minute too long.

••9. We must learn the lesson God wants to teach us••
	• We must submit to God's plan and trust Him to know what is best.
	• We must bring glory to God alone, even in the midst of trials.

••10. God is a good and loving Father••
	• He is not a cruel or capricious God, but a loving Father who wants the best for us.
	• He uses trials to refine us and prepare us for the life and service yet to come in heaven.

	• Peter presents Jesus Christ as the perfect example of one who suffered unjustly and obeyed God.
	• Jesus' death was a substitute for the unjust, bringing them to God.
• ••The Death of Christ••
	• Jesus suffered for well-doing, not because of His own sins.
	• He died as a substitute, and His death was a one-time event.
	• Jesus' death opened up access to God for believers.
• ••The Proclamation of Christ••
	• Jesus was "made alive by the Spirit" after His death.
	• This phrase is often misunderstood, but refers to the contrast between flesh and spirit.
	• Jesus' spirit died when He was made sin, but was later made alive.
• ••The Special Proclamation••
	• Jesus made a special proclamation to "the spirits in prison" after His death.
	• The identity and nature of these "spirits" is a topic of debate.
	• Some possible interpretations include:
		- Angels or demons
		- The spirits of lost sinners in hell
		- The spirits of the dead, awaiting resurrection
• ••The Meaning of "Spirits in Prison"••
	• The phrase "spirits in prison" is often misunderstood.
	• In the New Testament, "spirits" refers to angels or demons, not human beings.
	• The Bible does not teach that Jesus visited hell.
• ••The Realm of the Unbelieving Dead••
	• The word "hades" in Acts 2:31 refers to the realm of the unbelieving dead.
	• This is a temporary place where the dead await resurrection.
	• It is not the same as hell, which is the permanent and final place of judgment.
• ••The Purpose of Jesus' Proclamation••
	• The purpose of Jesus' proclamation to the spirits in prison is unclear.
	• Some possible interpretations include:
		- To bring salvation to those in prison
		- To demonstrate His power over the spirits in prison
		- To fulfill a specific purpose in the plan of God
• ••The Significance of Jesus' Death and Resurrection••
	• Jesus' death and resurrection are central to the Christian faith.
	• His death opened up access to God for believers.
	• His resurrection demonstrates His power over death and sin.

	• Understanding Jesus' ministry is crucial for suffering in the will of God.
